units.translation: Many Persian women they made bereft in vain, and husbandless.
Behold the offspring bereft of its father eagle
the foal of a dear husband, bereft
of which I have given goodwill, explaining
but with goodwill, how shall I accomplish an equal thing by speaking?
according to the goodwill of my heart
with the goodwill of Artemis the protectress
for everyone bears goodwill toward the weaker
Scythians, eaters of cheese made from mare's milk, dwelling in good pastures
But indeed the first judge of these dreams is well-disposed
into the hospitable men's halls of the house
This oracle is no longer easy to understand
easy to deal with / easy to conjecture
and to strangers easy to deal with, before arming Ares, may they grant justice without pains
this is easy for everyone to conjecture
first we pour forth from our mouths a good journey
and these things are in accordance with an oath
to feast on their own happiness in children
I am at a loss – a resourceful care
Lilaios, born of a noble father

with which compare the words of Athena 481: ἀμφότερα, μένειν πέμπειν τε τάσδε, πῆμ᾽ ἀμηχάνως τ᾽ ἔχει [both to remain and to send these away, and the trouble is unmanageable]. The scholiast explained it as εὐπαραίτητον, εὐχερῆ, εὐάρεστον [easy to be entreated, easy, easily pleased].
But these (Furies) have a portion not easily dismissed
both to remain and to send these away, and the trouble is unmanageable
easy to be entreated, easy, easily pleased
who is lord with swift foot of an easy leap
and to say it is easy, a pollution somehow
one might say that these things are easily
having easily cut off the heads of two serpents

In the places where the meter demands εὐπιθής [easily persuaded], it is probable that the same form should be restored in four other places (with Blomfield in his note on Pr. 341) where εὐπειθής [easily persuaded] is written, with the active meaning 'easily persuading'.

although εὐπειθής [easily persuaded] is quite frequent in other writers, as indicated in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 2385, and is not in itself to be rejected. For εὐπειθής [easily persuaded] is derived from the present, εὐπιθής [easily persuaded] from the aorist πιθεῖν [to persuade].
For you will not persuade him at all, for he is not easily persuaded
confidence easily persuaded sits on the dear throne of the heart
do you revere the easily persuaded apparitions of dreams?
what fair voyage did they accomplish with swift-sending pursuits?
